summary: “It’s this idea of dressing up. There will be characters that I have done as if we have made costumes.” Fashion’s long love affair with Hollywood was treated to full cinematic atmospherics by Jonathan Anderson last night at his first resort show for Dior. Under the soaring concrete arches of LACMA’s new David Geffen Galleries, complete with a scattering of vintage cars and film noir lighting effects by the movie industry’s finest, the models began moving from the far distance into focus. Dresses fluttering, tweeds glinting, feathered words perched on heads, it was a parade full of pretty things and plain-seeming things. There were asymmetric bias-cut satin slithers caught at the hip, Donegal Bar jackets dripping with disintegrating threads, chiffon whorled into rosettes, dresses smothered in 3-D poppy-heads, and choppy trailing boas. All these, mixed up with jeans (or what looked like them) and straightforward (although of course incredibly knowing and sophisticated) men’s shirts scattered with letters or numbers, a collaboration with the great American pop artist Ed Ruscha. The venue was of course a major scoop for Dior and LVMH. Also, the epicenter of a social scene which included a massive multigenerational cast of Hollywood guests from Al Pacino to Anna Taylor Joy, a lineup of movie costume greats and art world legends including Ruscha himself. Los Angeles is no stranger to major fashion shows, though. Many a designer has referenced old Hollywood and come to court the super-wealthy where they live, especially now that foreign travel may not be, shall we say, quite as attractive these days. cm-unit But with Anderson and Dior there are old histories and new plot-twists entwined in the relationship. In a preview, Anderson pulled out a pristine white version of a Christian Dior Bar jacket which the couturier had made for Marlene Dietrich. Dior designed her wardrobe for Alfred Hitchcock’s Stage Fright, for which he was nominated for a best costume Oscar in 1950. There was a kerfuffle over it: Dietrich had famously stipulated “No Dior, no Dietrich.” (And apparently, she kept the wardrobe afterward.) A quick check on Dior’s designs proves how some of Anderson’s free-flowing textile references may have originated in Dietrich’s pleated dresses, sparkling ballgown, and the extravagant overblown ruffles of her peignoir. But for Anderson, taking on Dior’s references and house codes is fashion as 3-D chess. “I think for me,” he said succinctly, “it’s about how do we—how do I—kind of historically rebuild the bedrock of Dior and then sort of dance on top of it.” That ‘dancing’ includes pulling on the legacies of all the designers who’ve passed through the house. Fashion nerds will spot the Galliano-isms in the bias cut dresses, and Anderson’s revival of the house saddle bag. To add to that, he demonstrated a soft suede shoulder bag with double straps, dating from a Marc Bohan design. The Ed Ruscha collab continues the tradition of the many artist-collaborations Kim Jones instituted at Dior Men. One personal Anderson-ism this season was his one-off commissioning of his boyhood Irish hero Philip Treacy to make the feather headpieces, simultaneously spelling out DIOR and Ruscha words—STAR, FLOW, BUZZ—whilst also paying respects to the late Isabella Blow, who so famously sported a Treacy original spelling her surname. Well, besides the collection and all its detailed delights (bejeweled ladybird and shamrock minaudières, among them), there was much more going on here behind the scenes. Anderson is a prime mover in the phenomenon of fashion-adjacent crossovers between art, craft, and filmmaking. His costume designs for Luca Guadagnino, and his friendship with the director are apparently about to yield another project, and—Anderson teased—there are two more in the works. “What you’re seeing here,” he said, “is part of a kind of broader picture of what we will do over the next 12 months in cinema. We’re in Hollywood, and we’re starting something, but it will be a larger picture thing that we will do with franchises, with film, with other things. So this is going to be like: how does a fashion house work with cinema? And how does the cinema work with a fashion house, and what is a new type of business model within that?” And all this, just one year into Anderson’s Dior tenure.
